analysis.one_liner: Lets tax-exempt and political groups keep their donors' names off IRS filings.
analysis.headline: All 48 of 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into permanent law a Trump-era rule that lets most tax-exempt organizations leave the names and addresses of their contributors off the annual returns they file with the IRS. It raises from $5,000 to $50,000 the income threshold below which groups are exempt from filing detailed reports, expands the categories of groups that qualify, and makes clear that political organizations (Section 527 groups, like PACs) are covered by the exemption. The practical effect is that money flowing to politically active nonprofits and political committees could stay hidden from public view, with only the IRS able to see it.
analysis.who_benefits: Large donors to politically active tax-exempt groups gain the most: their names and addresses would no longer appear on any annual IRS informational return, and 527 political organizations would be exempt from reporting substantial contributors. The organizations themselves benefit by avoiding donor-disclosure paperwork, and small charities benefit from the raised $50,000 threshold that spares them detailed filings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big political donors and advocacy nonprofits

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts from disclosure the names and addresses of contributors on tax-exempt organizations' annual informational returns [S2].
It raises the gross-receipts threshold for the reporting exemption from $5,000 to $50,000, sparing larger groups from detailed filings [S2].
It expands the exemption to cover all 501(c) organizations other than private foundations and supporting organizations, and to groups whose only activity is investment [S3].
It extends the reporting exemption to Section 527 political organizations, which would no longer have to report substantial contributors in the same way [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost in lost transparency: voters, journalists, and watchdogs would no longer be able to see who is bankrolling politically active nonprofits and political committees through annual IRS filings. The IRS also loses contributor data that helps it enforce tax rules against groups abusing their exempt status.

drawbacks.text: Removing donor names from annual returns means the public cannot see who funds organizations that lobby, run issue ads, and shape elections, because those groups would no longer have to report their contributors on those filings [S2].
The bill also covers Section 527 political organizations, which exist to influence elections, so contributor reporting for these committees would be narrowed as well [S2].

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: some small-group and minority donors have faced harassment when their giving to unpopular causes was exposed, and the bill's sponsor framed it as protecting taxpayers from the IRS being used against them; the bill's title reflects that concern [S1].

Raising the filing threshold from $5,000 to $50,000 means organizations with up to $50,000 in annual receipts no longer file detailed reports at all, which reduces information available about a much wider set of groups [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for small charities — less paperwork under a higher threshold — is real but modest. The larger effect runs the other way: the groups covered by the exemption include politically active 501(c) organizations and 527 election-focused committees, and the bill removes the main annual record of who funds them. For anyone trying to trace the money behind political advocacy, that is a significant loss of visibility, and it is not offset by anything in the bill that adds transparency elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill on May 20, 2021, with 44 other Republican senators joining as original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced [S1].
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll-call vote at any point after the referral [S5].
The bill gathered 48 cosponsors, all of them Republicans, out of the 50 Senate Republicans serving in the 117th Congress [S4].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill advancing out of committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the bill never became law, so existing contributor-reporting requirements in the tax code remained as they were. Public-transparency interests are better off that the bill died, while its donors and advocacy-group backers gained nothing beyond the Trump-era regulation it sought to lock in.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; disclosure rules stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the Republican conference behind it.

for.name: 48 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the Republican leader, but no floor vote ever occurred.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the record shows no committee action after the May 2021 referral.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: No Democratic senator cosponsored the bill, and the Democratic-controlled committee took no action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 cosponsors were Republicans — 48 of the 50 Senate Republicans — and no Democrat or independent signed on; the bill died in a Democratic-run committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Politically active 501(c) nonprofit groups (including 501(c)(4) 'social welfare' organizations)
industries.note: These groups would no longer have to name their contributors on annual IRS returns, so the money behind their lobbying and issue advocacy could stay hidden. Their gain — donor secrecy — comes directly at the public's cost in transparency about who is funding political influence.

The bill extends the reporting exemption to election-focused 527 organizations, which would no longer report substantial contributors in the same way as other filers. That shields the funding of election-influencing committees from public view.

Raising the filing threshold from $5,000 to $50,000 spares small groups detailed annual reporting. This is a genuine paperwork reduction for little community organizations, though it is a small share of the bill's overall effect.
